listing_view.reasoning: Subscription jumped from under 1x to ~13x on the final morning, which signals strong late demand and supports a listing-day pop. But the print was 0.86x the afternoon before close, meaning demand arrived only at the deadline — typical of momentum-chasing rather than fundamental conviction — and I have no grey-market, anchor, or OFS/fresh-issue data to test that surge.

longterm_view.reasoning: Revenue and PAT are both shrinking on a two-year view, ROE has fallen to 7.6% and ROCE to 10.6%, and the latest year's reported profit did not arrive as cash — operating cash flow was deeply negative while receivable days blew out from 35 to 137. A business compounding backwards, earning below cost-of-capital-type returns, and failing to convert profit to cash does not merit a positive long-term view at any price I can assess, and no valuation basis was provided to argue the price compensates.

governance.reasoning: SEBI has imposed a penalty on the company and issued a show-cause notice in its capacity as a registered investment adviser, and there is a further SEBI SCN on record [litigation, page 608][litigation, page 610]. One modest paid penalty plus unresolved regulatory notices is not disqualifying, but for a financial-services firm whose product is trust, it weighs negatively.

key_risks.risk: Profits are not converting to cash
key_risks.why_it_matters: Latest-year operating cash flow is deeply negative against ₹1,320m of reported PAT, meaning the earnings the IPO price is set against may exist only on paper.
Customers now take 137 days to pay versus 35 days two years ago, which is where the cash has gone and raises questions about revenue quality and collectibility.
The company, a SEBI-registered investment adviser, has a paid penalty and pending show-cause notices, so its licence-dependent revenue carries regulatory tail risk.
ROE at 7.6% and falling, with revenue down 24% in the latest year, means the business is deploying more capital to generate less profit.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: Receivables, demonstrably: collection stretched from 35 to 137 days and operating cash flow swung to roughly -₹1,970m in the latest year, so the profit is sitting in unpaid customer bills. Whether inventory also absorbed cash cannot be told — no inventory figure or working-capital breakdown was given.

answers.question: who are the customers, and is any of it disputed?
answers.answer: Not answerable from what I was given — the extracts name no customers and the only disputes disclosed are regulatory (SEBI penalty and show-cause notices), not customer disputes [litigation, page 608][litigation, page 610]. Given receivable days quadrupled, the absence of any customer-concentration or receivables-ageing disclosure in what I was shown is itself a gap, not reassurance.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that the receivables blowout is a one-off timing effect already collected post-period-end, plus disclosure of the customer base showing no concentration or dispute — that would repair the cash-conversion concern, which is the core of my negative long-term view. On listing, grey-market and anchor data could move the short-term score either way.
